transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-06
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Claire (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Jessie (Redwood SE), Aisha, Ben, Liam, Marta (Cobalt)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
- Deep technical discussion on multi-region routing, session affinity (sticky sessions), and KV cache eviction strategies for prefix caching.
- Evaluated tradeoffs: DNS vs Anycast, connection draining, warm pool sizes, dedicated vs hosted fallbacks, and quantization fallback for cold-start mitigation.
- Agreed to run benchmarks and draft DR tabletop playbook; several action items assigned.

Topics: Routing policy, regional capacity, sticky sessions, KV cache consistency/eviction, batching and quantization tradeoffs, VPC/private deployment implications, DR playbook steps.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Claire: hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we have about 50 minutes, want to make sure we focus on the sticky session behavior and eviction strategy that you called out in the ticket.
[00:22] Aisha: yeah thanks. we've had two incidents where traffic storms from EU region killed response latencies, rc—for us the KV cache warmed in us-east but eu-west cold, so failover was … kind of messy.
[00:38] Ravi: got it, can you say a bit about how your traffic is split today? is it geo-DNS, load balancer-based, or something like anycast?
[00:50] Ben: we're on geoDNS with a TTL of 60s, LB in front of the cluster per region. session affinity is sticky cookie-based at the LB level so some requests stick to the same region.
[01:12] Ravi: cool, that explains the sticky bits. two high-level knobs: route-by-latency vs route-by-cost vs route-by-capacity. we usually recommend policy routing with a primary region and an emergency fallback set — and prefer short TTLs for quick cutovers but that interacts with DNS resolver caching.
[01:40] Liam: when you say emergency fallback set, what happens to KV cache? if we switch region mid-session, are we going to stall on cold KV lookups?
[01:52] Jessie: great question, yes, if you move a live session to a region without the prefix cached you'll either hit a cold start or need to fetch from a remote store. we discussed three approaches: 1) shared KV (e.g., a regional Redis with cross-region replication), 2) proactive replication of hot prefixes to the warm pool in secondaries, 3) accept short latency spikes and rely on model-level quantized fallback to reduce token compute.
[02:25] Aisha: can you run through proactive replication? how do you avoid thrashing and over-replication?
[02:33] Ravi: sure — we track hot key heat via EWMA per-prefix. keys above threshold are bundled to an async replication queue; replicas in the secondary pull those prefixes into a warm cache. eviction policy on secondaries is LFU with a small max TTL and admission control so we don't replicate low-value prefixes.
[02:55] Ben: admission control sounds heavy — what's the overhead for metadata and propagation? do we need extra infrastructure?
[03:05] Ravi: minimal — metadata is lightweight counters. you can piggyback on the existing telemetry stream. replication is small compared to tokens since we only replicate KV blobs that correspond to hot prefixes, not full tensors.
[03:22] Marta: from a compliance standpoint, cross-region replication needs to be opt-in; we can't replicate EU PII into US. how do you handle residency?
[03:32] Claire: good, we support policy-based residency — replication rules are scoped by data label. also Redwood Private gives you control for on-prem or VPC options so replication can be disabled entirely.
[03:45] Aisha: ok. what about session stickiness? our LB sticky cookie means some users continue to hit a degraded region during a partial outage.
[03:56] Ravi: two patterns: short-lived affinity (e.g., 30s) with token-aware routing, or sticky at app-level with session handoff. For degraded region, we prefer a weighted traffic-split where the policy marks region as degraded and shifts percentage of new sessions to fallback regions; existing sticky sessions are drained or explicitly migrated if you implement state transfer.
[04:18] Ben: explicit migration — that sounds complex. how would you do that?
[04:24] Jessie: the pragmatic path is 'drain then migrate': stop new session creates in degraded region, let existing sessions finish up (bounded by max session TTL), and for long-running ones you either replicate state (complex) or spawn a proxy that routes session reads to primary cache over private link.
[04:41] Liam: proxying remote reads under load seems risky — will that blow latency SLAs?
[04:46] Ravi: yep, it's risky — that's why warm pooling and proactive replication are the more resilient options for low-latency apps.
[04:54] Claire: quick aside on DNS: lowering TTL helps faster failover but amplifies DNS query volume and makes client resolvers (ISP caches) more visible; we've seen resolvers ignore very low TTLs. so we combine short TTLs with route-by-application health checks and a control plane orchestrated change instead of relying on DNS alone.
[05:18] Aisha: do you support Anycast? we've been evaluating Anycast for instant cutover.
[05:24] Ravi: we support Anycast-style routing where the edge routes to nearest healthy region, but Anycast eliminates control granularity — you get fast failover but lose fine-grained per-customer routing and it's harder with VPC/private deployments. Plus Anycast TTL for sticky sessions is tricky.
[05:41] Ben: ok. let's talk about batching and quantization during failover — you mentioned we could fall back to a smaller quantized variant to reduce latency spikes?
[05:50] Jessie: right. two levers during overload: reduce batch windows (sacrifices throughput), or route to a quantized/FP16-int8 variant that is cheaper and faster but may have small quality regressions. you can do dynamic model switching per-policy and tie it to error budgets.
[06:10] Liam: how do you validate quality regressions? we can't have hallucination regressions in clinical contexts.
[06:16] Ravi: best practice: have an eval set (we call them sentinel prompts) and continuous quality monitors. during canary we run shadow traffic against quantized variant and watch delta metrics — perplexity/levenshtein, domain-specific scoring — and only route production traffic if deltas are within thresholds.
[06:34] Aisha: about the playbook — what are the concrete runbook steps for a region outage? we need actionable ops steps.
[06:42] Claire: high-level playbook steps we propose: 1) detection and triage (automated alerts + SRE ack), 2) isolate degraded region, 3) shift new session traffic via policy (control plane), 4) enable warm pool replication if not already: prefetch top-n prefixes, 5) reduce model batch window and/or switch to quantized fallback, 6) monitor quality and roll back when stable, 7) post-mortem and cache rebalance.
[07:10] Ben: detection — how fast can Redwood's control plane mark a region unhealthy and shift traffic?
[07:16] Ravi: normal is sub-10s for internal health checks and sub-minute for provider-side conditions once thresholds are crossed. actual cutover depends on resolver TTLs and your client behavior; but in our experience, with control-plane enforced routing you can see effective traffic shift in 30–90s.
[07:35] Aisha: client SDK behavior matters — our mobile apps cache endpoint IPs aggressively; does Redwood provide an SDK to force re-resolve?
[07:43] Claire: we provide an SDK with a re-resolve hook and sticky session helpers; you can trigger a re-resolve or bump an SDK version that honors health signals.
[07:52] Liam: let's dig into eviction specifics — what's your recommended TTL and eviction policy for region caches?
[07:59] Ravi: recommended is hybrid: LRU for local evictions with LFU admission for replicated items. TTLs depend on your prefix churn — we suggest 10–30 minutes for hot prefixes, with heat decay based on EWMA so cold traffic falls out quickly. important to cap warm pool size per-region to control memory.
[08:24] Ben: and for long tail queries that are rare?
[08:28] Jessie: serve from source (e.g., shared blob store), but have a slow-path that uses a quantized model to reduce cost. also you can async-populate the prefix into warm pool after first hit.
[08:38] Aisha: what's the best metric to gate replication? is it QPS per-key?
[08:44] Ravi: QPS, combined with recency and value (cost of miss). we compute a hotness score: hotness = alpha * QPS + beta * recency_score - gamma * cost_of_replication. thresholds tuned per workload.
[08:58] Liam: any operational examples of a time when replication created thrash? want to avoid thundering herd.
[09:05] Ravi: yes, if you naively replicate everything you see spikes. admission control + backoff helps: replicate only when hot for two consecutive windows; use jittered backoffs for replicas to avoid simultaneous large writes.
[09:20] Ben: can you demo that logic or share pseudo-code?
[09:23] Ravi: yes I'll share the pseudo-code and the spreadsheet with simulated thresholds.
[09:27] (short pause, typing noise)
[09:45] Aisha: okay, quick side question — for Private deployments inside our VPC, does the runbook change? we can't accept cross-region replication without approved link.
[09:55] Claire: for Private, we still offer the same controls but replication must go over your private interconnect or be disabled. the control plane can orchestrate policies but the data plane replication happens over your network.
[10:10] Marta: from a compliance standpoint we'd prefer policy that keeps PII local and replicates only non-PII prefixes. possible?
[10:17] Ravi: yes, label-based replication rules are supported. you can tag prefixes or models as nonreplicable and the policy engine will block replication.
[10:25] Liam: training vs inference — not relevant here but can quantized fallback be configured per-model? we use a family of models.
[10:33] Jessie: yes per-model fallbacks and per-route profiles. you can specify a fallback chain: full-precision -> FP16 -> 8-bit quantized -> smaller model. each step has perf/quality metadata.
[10:45] Ben: during failover do you recommend switching batch windows immediately or gradual?
[10:50] Ravi: gradual: reduce batch window in steps and monitor latency percentiles. sudden shrink can increase cost and reduce throughput unpredictably. tie it to queue depth and latency SLO thresholds.
[11:03] Aisha: curious about KV consistency. what's the model for cross-region replication? eventual or strongly consistent?
[11:08] Ravi: it's eventual for performance reasons. we provide best-effort sync and a read-repair mechanism for critical keys. if you need strong consistency you can fall back to a central store but expect higher latencies.
[11:23] Liam: read-repair sounds good — can you describe a real-world reconcilation?
[11:28] Ravi: read-repair example: if a secondary serves a key not matching primary version, the secondary will fetch authoritative blob asynchronously and update cache, then emit an inconsistency alert. for very sensitive keys we tag them and route reads to the authoritative region.
[11:44] Ben: what about cache warming during scale-ups — e.g., we spin up a standby region to handle seasonal spikes. what's the warm-up strategy?
[11:52] Jessie: warm-up strategies: prefetch top-k prefixes (based on historical heat), run synthetic traffic via replayed representative prompts to warm KV and KV-to-model path, and use background cold-spot sampling to populate mid-tier popularity.
[12:10] Aisha: does Redwood support replaying masked traffic for privacy? we can't re-run real PII.
[12:17] Claire: yes, we have a masked-replay tool that hashes or mutes PII and replays structural features. it produces representative cache warm-up without PII leakage.
[12:29] Liam: about throttling — if we shift traffic abruptly, do you have circuit-breakers at model route level?
[12:36] Ravi: yes we have circuit-breakers by route and by model. they can trip on error rates, latency, or token-cost. when tripped, policy either routes to fallback model or returns a degraded-but-safe response.
[12:50] Ben: can we attach a manual override? during a DR we'd like an SRE to manually trigger a policy.
[12:57] Claire: absolutely — control plane supports manual overrides, canaries, and scheduled rollbacks.
[13:05] Aisha: can we walk through a hypothetical incident timeline? say EU region goes to 200% latency at 13:00, what's the timeline?
[13:12] Ravi: quick sketch: 13:00 detect spike -> 13:01 automated alert -> 13:02 control-plane marks region degraded -> 13:03 shift new sessions to fallback via control plane (clients that re-resolve) -> 13:04 SDK re-resolve hooks accelerating client rebind -> 13:04-13:06 warm-pool replication kicks in for top-k prefixes -> 13:06 reduce batch window and enable quantized fallback for high-latency routes -> 13:06-13:15 monitor and adjust. full remediation usually within 10–20 minutes for most cases.
[13:47] Liam: that timeline assumes clients do re-resolve. what if mobile clients don't?
[13:52] Jessie: then control-plane level proxying can intercept and route, but that requires traffic to flow through a managed edge; for private-only networks you need an SDK update or LB rule change.
[14:05] Ben: any guidance on warm-pool sizing? how many prefixes?
[14:09] Ravi: rule of thumb: warm-pool size = top_n where top_n covers 80% of request volume; often top 5-10k prefixes depending on application. memory budget and prefix size vary a lot. run a command on your logs to compute the Pareto coverage.
[14:32] Aisha: ok let's pivot to the DR tabletop — what do you recommend we rehearse?
[14:38] Claire: rehearse detection, control-plane failover, SDK rebind, warm-up, quantized fallback, rollback, and post-mortem. make sure roles are assigned: who hits the manual override, who monitors quality, who talks to compliance.
[14:54] Ben: roles — SRE will handle manual override, platform owner will validate quality metrics, and legal/compliance will be on-call for data residency checks.
[15:03] Liam: on the topic of monitoring, what are the minimum metrics we should surface?
[15:08] Ravi: minimal set: per-region p99 latency, p50, error-rate, token-rate, cache hit-rate per-prefix, warm-pool size, replication lag, model fallback percentage, and sentinel prompt quality delta.
[15:30] Aisha: how do sentinel prompts look? do you have a template?
[15:35] Jessie: yes, we'll share a template: domain-specific prompts, edge-case hallucination checks, and safety guardrails. we run them every minute against shadowed traffic.
[15:46] (typing)
[16:00] Ben: ok, shifting gears: we've been using a 4GB KV blob size limit; is that reasonable for your warm pool?
[16:07] Ravi: depends — 4GB per key is huge; usually KV blobs for model prefix/context are in the order of KBs to low MBs. if you have 4GB blobs you might be storing entire session transcripts which we'd recommend offload to object store and only keep compressed context in KV.
[16:24] Aisha: noted. also curious about costs — what does warm-pool replication cost vs token cost?
[16:31] Claire: warm-pool replication is mostly memory and inter-region bandwidth; token cost is compute-heavy. in many cases replicating a small hot prefix is cheaper than paying repeated cold-start model tokens. we'll share a cost spreadsheet with ballpark numbers.
[16:48] Liam: show of hands — are there any questions about quantization drift over time? we've seen degradation in some domain-specific metrics.
[16:55] Jessie: quantization drift can happen if model internals change; mitigate with regular re-evals and a rolling recalibration job. also keep a lineup of fallback models and retrain quantized variants periodically.
[17:10] Ben: for lab testing, can we run a synthetic DR where we flip region to 0% and observe client behavior?
[17:15] Ravi: absolutely — we can run a controlled experiment in staging: simulate region outage, run load test (locust-like) with SDK set to not re-resolve to measure proxy path, then re-run with SDK re-resolve to measure best-case.
[17:29] Aisha: perfect. can you include the test harness and commands?
[17:33] Ravi: yes will include in the doc.
[17:36] (5-minute deeper whiteboard discussion on pseudo-code, omitted by transcript)
[22:50] Claire: picking back up — two remaining items: eviction jittering and back-pressure to prevent a thundering heat when a region recovers.
[22:58] Ravi: eviction jitter: we apply random TTL offsets on eviction to spread rehydration. back-pressure: if replicas are saturating network, we slow replication with token-bucket pacing and prioritize top-k prefixes.
[23:12] Ben: do we need a separate replication queue per-region?
[23:16] Ravi: yes per-region queue with global coordinator to avoid hotspots.
[23:22] Liam: if we lose one region and then it recovers, how do you rebalance cache back? do you evict duplicates?
[23:29] Jessie: rebalancing strategy: once primary healthy, you can either let secondaries expire naturally or proactively rehydrate primary and drain secondaries. proactive approach: replicate back most recent authoritative keys, then gradually shift traffic. we avoid mass-eviction to reduce flapping.
[23:48] Aisha: any gotchas with dedicated capacity and keepalive connections across regions?
[23:54] Claire: keepalives are per-region; cross-region keepalive means you need private network and careful connection draining policies. also watch for ephemeral port exhaustion when proxying traffic.
[24:08] Ben: what about TLS termination across regions — should we terminate at edge or region?
[24:12] Ravi: terminate at the edge that you control. for Private, you may want regional termination with mTLS to internal services. certificate rotation needs to be automated.
[24:24] Liam: ok. are we missing any compliance / audit items for the playbook?
[24:29] Marta: need to ensure audit logs for any policy change (manual override), replication toggles, and who viewed PII-labeled keys. we also need an encrypted audit trail in our SIEM.
[24:41] Claire: Redwood records control-plane events and can forward audit logs to your SIEM; we'll provide retention options as an add-on.
[24:51] Aisha: moving on — can we do a quick recap of the concrete configuration we'd propose for Cobalt?
[24:58] Ravi: proposed config (high level): geo-routing with policy-based primary EU-west1, fallback to US-east1, short DNS TTL 60s plus SDK re-resolve hook, warm-pool in primary and secondary with top-5k prefixes, EWMA-based replication admission, LFU admission on replicas, backoff/jitter on replication, quantized fallback chain (FP16 -> 8-bit), circuit-breakers by route, and manual override channel in control plane.
[25:30] Ben: sounds good. what about size of warm-pool memory estimate?
[25:34] Ravi: rough calc: average prefix size 20KB * 10k prefixes = ~200MB plus overhead, so under 1GB in many cases. we'll refine once you share sample data.
[25:48] Aisha: ok. next steps and timelines covered earlier. anything else?
[25:55] Liam: one last nit: is there an API to query per-prefix heat in real time?
[26:01] Claire: yes there's a telemetry API and a dashboard; we'll share read-only credentials for staging.
[26:07] (quiet typing)
[26:22] Ben: thanks everybody this was helpful.
[26:25] Claire: great, we'll wrap and send the doc.
[26:29] Ravi: I'll attach the pseudo-code and the simulation spreadsheet.
[26:33] Jessie: I'll add the warm-up script and the canary playbook.
[26:36] Aisha: thanks, look forward to the tabletop.
[26:40] (call ends)
